albums.blurb: Sven Wunder is the pseudonym of a deliberately elusive Stockholm multi-instrumentalist who recreates the sound of 1970s European library music, one theme per album: Turkish psych-folk on Eastern Flowers (2019), Japanese scales on Wabi Sabi (2020). Natura Morta, his third album on his own Piano Piano label, turns to the Italian soundtrack tradition — eleven short instrumentals, each named for a still-life motif, scored for jazz rhythm section with strings, flute, harp, and harpsichord.
albums.reception: The Quietus's review called it "a record drenched in colour and luxuriously rich in melody, beautifully played, arranged, and recorded."

albums.blurb: Third album from the London duo of Josh Lloyd-Watson and Tom McFarland, and their first on their own Caiola Records after leaving XL. It is also the first Jungle record with outside voices — rapper Bas and Tamil-Swiss singer Priya Ragu guest — and it trades the moodier tempos of For Ever (2018) for brisk strings-and-falsetto disco cut for the dance floor.
albums.reception: It debuted at No. 3 on the UK Albums Chart, topped Billboard's Top Dance/Electronic Albums chart, and holds a Metacritic score of 81 from 11 reviews.

albums.blurb: Fela Kuti was the Nigerian saxophonist and bandleader who, with drummer Tony Allen and the Afrika 70 band, invented Afrobeat: long-form grooves stacking tight horn riffs, hypnotic rhythm guitar, and call-and-response vocals. Zombie, released in Nigeria in 1976 and internationally in 1977, is the sharpest political statement in his vast catalog — the title track mocks Nigerian soldiers as zombies who obey without thinking, and the record so enraged the military government that roughly a thousand soldiers stormed and burned his Kalakuta commune in 1977.
albums.reception: AllMusic calls it his most popular and impactful record, Pitchfork ranked it No. 90 among the 100 best albums of the 1970s, and Robert Christgau graded it A−, hailing it as "real fusion music."
